screeningSummary: Son clearing out his late father's workshop found a sealed envelope - a 1966 photo, an unsigned typed page, a clipped article
arcNotes: Question arc with grief at the center: 'did the government pay him to be quiet?' Vern shares the Blue Book-era kitchen-table culture (rank and fear, not money - the Robertson Panel's de-escalation advice), then reframes: a sealed envelope with a readable date is a man betting his son would open it right. Ends with the reading-on-air promise

lines.text: He died in April. We were clearing his workshop, and behind the paint cans there was an envelope - sealed, no name on it. Inside: a photograph of a light over our farm, dated 1966 on the print's edge. A typed page with no signature. And a newspaper clipping about the Air Force project. My dad never said one word about any of it. Not one word in fifty years. Did they pay him to be quiet?

lines.text: He kept it from you - and I'll tell you what my files say about 1966, because your father's page reads like every other file from that decade. There was a time when Air Force men sat at kitchen tables and asked farmers to keep quiet - not with money, usually. With rank. And with fear. A panel of scientists in the fifties advised the government to talk sightings down, to make witnesses feel foolish, and the officers followed the advice. Witnesses learned that talking meant the men in uniform came back. Nobody had to be paid. A man who loved his son kept a secret for fifty years because one visit convinced him the secret was keeping his boy safe. That's not a payoff. That's worse - that's love wearing a uniform's advice.

lines.text: He withheld it from you - and the archive contextualizes 1966: your father's page matches the decade's pattern precisely. Air Force personnel conducted kitchen-table interviews requesting discretion - enforcement via rank and fear rather than payment. A 1950s scientific panel recommended minimizing public interest and ridiculing witnesses; officers implemented the recommendation. Witnesses learned disclosure prompted return visits. No compensation was required. A father convinced that silence protected his son maintained it for fifty years. That is not a payoff - it is affection operating under institutional pressure.

lines.text: He was keeping it for you - and he left you the key, because a sealed envelope with a readable date isn't a man taking a secret to his grave. It's a man betting his son would be curious enough, and careful enough, to open it right. So open it right: don't handle the photograph more than you have to. Keep everything in that envelope until an investigator or an archive can date the paper and the print together. 1966, a light over a farm, a typed page - that's a case file from the old era with a family witness attached, and those almost never survive. His did. You're holding your father's only statement now, and the question isn't whether they paid him. It's where his words go next.
